content.title: No nurse left behind
content.subtitle: Continuous Professional Development of nurses and midwives throughout Kenya
content.summary: AKU-SONAM delivers Continuous Professional Development courses to nurses and midwives around Kenya

content.text: Nurses and midwives work on the frontlines to provide healthcare. This means they hardly get time to grow their careers or catch up on the latest innovations or trends in healthcare. According to

, 44% of nurses and midwives find it challenging to commit time to pursue professional development. Those working in community settings, public health facilities and in secondary care, struggle to fit Continuous Professional Development (CPD) courses in their schedules. They frequently work past their shift due to understaffing and have to see an overwhelming number of patients, leaving little time to focus on their professional development.

AKU's School of Nursing and Midwifery (AKU-SONAM) understands this challenge and works with county governments and healthcare facilities in East Africa to deliver CPD short courses. These courses aim to ensure that working nurses and midwives are efficient in healthcare delivery and acquainted with best practices in the profession. The courses are developed and facilited by the faculty across the region and are offered for free thanks to a partnership with the German Development Bank (KfW).

Before the short courses are developed, an assessment of the needs of the counties and respective health facilities is carried out. The courses entail taking participants through effective communication with doctors, chemotherapy safety, principles of infection control, leadership, how to handle work-related violence among others.

Beth Waweru is the CPD coordinator at AKU-SONAM Kenya. Together with CPD associate Ordinah Bukachi and other faculty, they have trained over 900 participants in Kenya, going as far as Turkana, 609km from Nairobi. However, the training can come with challenges.

Beth vividly remembers a session at a hospital in Kiambu County which took place during a challenging time for the institution. Personnel at the hospital had just been accused of negligence after a three-month-old baby had to have his arm and leg amputated due to a BCG vaccination that went wrong. This attracted media attention with journalists camping outside the hospital. Staff were to scared to walk out because no one wanted to address the media. Beth's workshop focused on how healthcare workers can improve communication among themselves to ensure that such occurences are prevented. "I went on with the training because I didn't think it was right to abandon them during such an uncertain time. When things go wrong is when nurses need to be trained so that they learn how to be better for the next patients," Beth said.
The courses have had a real impact even in remote areas such as Turkana in northern Kenya.

After Beth and her team had completed their workshop in Turkana, the Chief Nursing Officer of Turkana County, Margaret Lokota, shared that "It is commendable to see the change in our nurses who were trained by AKU. They have given positive feedback to the administration and are also training their colleagues. We have seen a huge change and would wish to continue working with AKU-SONAM to strengthen the capacity of our nurses."

Some of the institutions that have received training include St Francis Community Hospital, Mathari Teaching and Referral Hospital, Mombasa Hospital, Coast General Hospital, Kiambu Level V Hospital, Kihara Hospital, Shalom Group of Hospitals among others.
